**Student:** I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿All praise is due to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light. Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾ (1) ﴿It is He who created you from clay, then decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him. Yet you still doubt.﴾ (2) ﴿And He is God in the heavens and on the earth. He knows what you conceal and what you reveal, and He knows what you earn.﴾ [al-An'am 1-3].

**The Shaykh:** I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. In the last lesson we began speaking about the basmalah (the formula "In the name of God..."), did we not?

**Students:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** We reached His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿In the name of God﴾ [al-Fatihah 1]. We mentioned that this mighty name is the root of the names, and that no one is called by it except God, mighty and majestic is He.

As for His saying ﴿the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)﴾: al-Rahman is derived from "mercy" (al-rahmah), but it is in the pattern (fa'lan), and this pattern indicates breadth and abundance. Its meaning is therefore that He possesses vast mercy. For this reason some scholars explained it as "the One of general mercy," but the correct view is that He is the One of vast mercy, who shows mercy to whomever He wills, mighty and majestic is He. So it is more indicative of a description than of an action; it is more indicative of God's attribute than of an act. As for al-Rahim (the Especially Merciful), it is also an intensive form derived from mercy, but it is more indicative of an action than of a description. Al-Rahman therefore precedes, because it is a description, and al-Rahim follows, because it is an action. Thus He is al-Rahman, who shows mercy, mighty and majestic is He.

God, blessed and exalted, has also said that He is merciful to the believers (ﷻ, Qur'an 33:43), and the intended meaning there is special mercy.

So al-Rahman indicates what? A description. And al-Rahim indicates an action, meaning that He shows mercy.

The scholars, may God have mercy on them, divided mercy into two kinds: general and special. General mercy is that which encompasses all creatures: the believer and the disbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, the small and the great, the animal and the rational. All creatures are under God's mercy, mighty and majestic is He, and no one departs from this general mercy. Special mercy is that which is specific to the believers. The difference between them is that special mercy is connected to the mercy of the Hereafter, so God, mighty and majestic, has mercy upon the believers both in this world and in the Hereafter. General mercy, however, has no effect except in this world.

For this reason we say: the disbelievers in the Hereafter are treated with justice, not with mercy. Animals and non-rational creatures are likewise treated with justice, because God judges between them, between the animals, and then says to them: "Be dust," and they become dust. We do not understand... So how many kinds is mercy?

**A student:** Two kinds.

**The Shaykh:** Two kinds, or two divisions: general, which encompasses all creatures, and special, which is specific to the believers. The difference between them is that the general is only in this world, while the special is in this world and the Hereafter. O God, have mercy upon us through Your mercy.

The mention of these two noble names at the basmalah, which precedes the servant's act and speech, is an indication that if God does not show you mercy, you will gain nothing from this act or this speech. For this reason the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, said: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God envelops me with His mercy." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5673), Muslim (2816/71), from Abu Hurayrah.]

He said: ﴿All praise is due to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. The article (al) here is for totality (al-istighraq), meaning that all praise, in every respect, belongs to God, mighty and majestic is He. The preposition "li" in His saying ﴿to God﴾ may indicate exclusivity (al-ikhtisas) or entitlement (al-istihqaq), and there is no contradiction between the two meanings. So it indicates entitlement and exclusivity, because the article in ﴿al-hamd (all praise)﴾ is for generality, and no one deserves all praise in its generality except God, mighty and majestic. Thus the "li" is for entitlement and also for exclusivity.

But what is praise (al-hamd)? Many people define it as "praise for a beautiful voluntary quality," but this is not correct, because praise (al-thana') is repetition of praise. The evidence for this is His saying, blessed and exalted, in the hadith qudsi (a hadith in which God speaks in the first person): "When the servant says: ﴿All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, God says: 'My servant has praised Me.' And when he says: ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, He says: 'He has extolled Me.'" [Muslim (395/38), from Abu Hurayrah.] This indicates that praise (al-thana') is the repetition of a complete description, and the derivation supports this, because al-thana' comes from al-thani, which means repeating a thing or turning part of a thing back to another part. As for their saying "for a beautiful voluntary quality," it is also not correct regarding God, mighty and majestic is He, because God is praised for what He does, and He chooses what He wills, and He is praised for the perfection of His necessary attributes, which do not extend to anyone else. So He is praised for the perfection of His life, and praised for the perfection of His self-subsistence (al-qayyumiyyah). The first is a necessary attribute, and the second is a transitive attribute that is also necessary, as explained earlier.

So the correct view is that praising God is for His actions which He chooses, and for His perfect attributes which are necessary to Him. How then do we define it? We say: praise (al-hamd) is describing the one praised with perfection, out of love and exaltation. This is because one may describe a person with perfection without loving him, but out of hope for what he will reward you with; and one may praise someone not out of love and exaltation, but out of fear of his harm. Therefore praise must be qualified as being out of love and exaltation. If it is not out of love and exaltation, it is mere praise (al-madh).

Consider the depth of the Arabic language, how it distinguished between hamd and madh while they are similar in letters, both in type and number. There are three letters: this is the number, and the type is the same letters (ḥā', mīm, dāl), but the order of the letters differs (ḥamd and madh), and as the order differs, their meanings differ. The relation between them is one of specificity and generality: every hamd is madh, but not every madh is hamd, because hamd, as we said, must be out of love and exaltation, whereas madh is otherwise. A man may praise a ruler or a minister, or something similar, without love or exaltation for him, but hoping for his gift or fearing him. But hamd is not like that.

Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, mentioned the differences between them in his book Bada'i' al-Fawa'id, which our Shaykh urged us to study when seeking knowledge, and he said: it is a great book. It resembles, in some respects, Sayd al-Khatir by Ibn al-Jawzi, but in depth, meaning, and benefit, there is no comparison. He, may God have mercy on him, clearly explained the differences between "hamd" and "madh," and examined this topic until he refined it thoroughly.

And he said: our Shaykh, meaning Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, when he investigated such matters, brought wondrous marvels, may God have mercy on him, but as it is said:

"The lightning flashed from Najd, so I said to it: Away from me, for I am preoccupied (with other things)."

Because Shaykh al-Islam had no leisure to speak about such matters. He spoke about what is greater. Our brother and colleague Farid ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Zamil collected the grammatical discussions that Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah addressed into a treatise, but it has not yet been published. This is good. Something of this kind also appeared to us in the book Iqtida' al-Sirat al-Mustaqim, when he discussed God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you plunged in as they plunged﴾ [al-Tawbah 69]. He investigated it in a way you will not find in any other book, may God have mercy on him.

But to return to our subject: hamd is describing the praised one with perfection, out of love and exaltation.

As for ﴿to God (lillah)﴾: we said the "li" is for entitlement and exclusivity. No one deserves all praise in every respect except God, mighty and majestic is He. This praise mentioned is specific to God, mighty and majestic is He, so He, exalted is He, is worthy of being praised, and complete praise belongs exclusively to Him.

As for "Allah," it is a proper name for God, mighty and majestic is He, and using it is better than using anything else. Some people now say: "The Truth (al-Haqq) said such-and-such," "The Truth said such-and-such." This is true, since God is the Manifest Truth, but make your expression follow the expression of the early generation (al-salaf), who say: "God said," or they say: "Our Lord said." As for "The Truth said," a person uses it in order to open minds so that the listener asks: "Who is this Truth?" But saying "God said" is better, since on it is built divinity and worship. Yet there is no harm in saying "Our Lord said" or "Your Lord said," as the Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, sometimes said to his companions: "Do you know what your Lord said?" [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (846), Muslim (71/125), from Zayd ibn Khalid.]

﴿Allah﴾: it is derived from divinity (al-uluhiyyah), and (ʾalaha) means "to worship," not "to be bewildered," as some claimed, because when a person says "Allah," he finds no bewilderment; he finds a known Lord, mighty and majestic is He, with no confusion in Him. They say its original form is (al-ilah), but the hamzah was dropped due to frequent usage.

They also said that its counterpart is (al-nas, people), whose original form is (al-unas), and the words (khayr, better) and (sharr, worse), whose original forms are (akhyar) and (ashrar).

So ﴿Allah﴾ originally is (al-ilah), and it comes from (alaha), meaning "he worshipped Him." Is it derived or fixed (jamid)?

The correct view is that it is derived, and that no name of God, nor name of the Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, nor name of the Qur'an, is ever fixed (jamid), because a fixed noun means that it has no meaning except to designate a specific referent. Because a proper noun, as Ibn Malik said:

"A noun that designates the named absolutely, its being a proper name, like Ja'far and Khirnaq."

So if we said that the names of God, or the names of the Messenger, or the names of the Noble Book are fixed, that would mean they indicate only the designation of the named. But we say: they are derived, indicating the designation of the named and also the meaning from which they are derived, necessarily.

So ﴿Allah﴾ is derived from (al-ilah) or (al-uluhiyyah), which is worship of God, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿Who created the heavens and the earth﴾: ﴿Who (alladhi)﴾ is a descriptive clause (sifah) of the divine name.

﴿created the heavens and the earth﴾: ﴿created (khalaqa)﴾ means brought into being according to a firm measure, because the basic meaning of creation (khalq) in the language is measuring (taqdir), as the poet said:

"Indeed you tear apart what you have measured, while people measure and do not tear (it apart)."

(yafri) means "to do."
(tafri ma khalaqta) means "what you have measured," and no one can prevent you. So creation is bringing into being in a firmly measured manner.

As for His saying ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾: ﴿the heavens (al-samawat)﴾ is the object of ﴿created﴾. There is no objection to saying it is the object, contrary to those who said it is not valid as an object, because the object must be the thing on which the verb acts, and it exists, and the creation of the heavens and the earth acted upon them before they were created. But we say this is far-fetched, and the correct view, which most grammarians (al-mu'rabin) hold, is that ﴿al-samawat﴾ is the direct object.

﴿created the heavens and the earth﴾: ﴿al-samawat﴾ is from (sama, yasmu), meaning "to rise high." God has made clear that they are seven, that they are layered (tibaq), that they are strong (shidad), and that they were built with hands, meaning with power.

His saying ﴿and the earth (al-ard)﴾ is conjoined to ﴿al-samawat﴾, and it is a singular noun, but that does not prevent plurality when it is established that it is plural.

Pay attention to this qualification: it does not prevent plurality if it is established that it is plural. And if it were not established that they are plural, we would say they are singular, because that is what the wording implies. But we say that the intended meaning is the genus, and in that case it does not contradict plurality. It is plural according to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the clear statement of the Sunnah. As for the Qur'an, God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them﴾ [al-Talaq 12], meaning in number. No one could say that ﴿the like of them (of the earth)﴾ refers to the manner or attributes, because the difference between the heaven and the earth is clear. So the intended meaning must be the number, and that is so.

As for the Sunnah, it is explicit. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever unjustly seizes a span of land, God will collar him with it on the Day of Resurrection, from seven earths." [Muslim (1610/137), from Sa'id ibn Zayd.] So the intended meaning of "earth" is the genus, and this does not contradict plurality. The plurality of the earths is established by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the clear statement of the Sunnah: they are seven.

﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾: ﴿made (ja'ala)﴾ means "created (khalaqa)." But if it means "created," what is the wisdom in expressing creation by "making"?

It has been said that the wisdom is variety in expression; that is, changing the wording while the meaning remains the same is sometimes part of eloquence.

It has also been said that the wisdom is that light cannot exist except through something else. For example, the light of the sun cannot be perceived unless there is a body that receives it. For this reason, between us and the sun there is darkness, because light cannot have its effect unless it falls upon a body.

You can now see the difference between the sun shining upon a body that receives heat and a body that does not, and between a body that receives brightness of whiteness and one that does not. Light cannot exist by itself, and it is not manifest unless it is reflected upon a body. This is the wisdom in His saying ﴿made﴾.

Another wisdom: darknesses and light are both sensory and immaterial, are they not? What is the darkness of the night?

**A student:** Sensory.

**The Shaykh:** Sensory. What about the darkness of ignorance?

**The students:** Immaterial.

**The Shaykh:** The darkness of ignorance is immaterial. Likewise light: the light of day is sensory, and the light of knowledge and faith is immaterial. From the light of knowledge and faith is the illumination of the heart by the speech of God, mighty and majestic is He, and the speech of God, exalted is He, is uncreated, although the Qur'an is called light, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ [al-Nisa' 174]. Is that clear? Therefore God, mighty and majestic is He, expressed it by "making," because it relates both to the created and to the uncreated.

﴿and made the darknesses and the light; then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am 1]: ﴿then (thumma)﴾ is a well-known conjunctive particle, and it indicates coordination and delay. If you wish, say: it indicates sequence and delay. So the meaning of the verse is: then, despite the manifestation of this matter, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth and the making of the darknesses and the light, despite this, those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord, despite the manifestation of the signs. There is no doubt that the disbelief of disbelievers in spite of the manifest signs deserves greater blame and rebuke than that of those who are not in such a position.

As for His saying ﴿disbelieved in their Lord﴾: is ﴿in their Lord (bi-rabbihim)﴾ to be connected to ﴿disbelieved (kafaru)﴾, or to ﴿ascribe equals (ya'dilun)﴾?

The structure allows that ﴿disbelieved in their Lord﴾ and ﴿ascribe equals﴾ means they make others equal to Him. It is also possible that ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ is separated from His saying ﴿in their Lord they ascribe equals﴾, and the meaning would be that those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord, that is, they make something other than God equal to God, blessed and exalted is He.

* * *

**Student:** I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿All praise is due to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾ (1) ﴿It is He who created you from clay, then decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him; yet you still doubt.﴾ (2) ﴿And He is God in the heavens and on the earth. He knows what you conceal and what you reveal, and He knows what you earn.﴾ [al-An'am 1-3].

**The Shaykh:** I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. God, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿All praise is due to God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. The explanation of this whole sentence was already given. ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾. Here we stopped.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 6, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord.﴾ That is: after these great, manifest and clear signs, those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord, meaning they make others equal to Him, setting up rivals (nidd) to Him.

Regarding His saying ﴿those who disbelieve in their Lord ascribe equals﴾: is the prepositional phrase ﴿in their Lord﴾ attached to ﴿disbelieve﴾ or to ﴿ascribe equals﴾?

The better view is that it is attached to ﴿ascribe equals﴾ (ya'dilūna), because this is the meaning that fits. As for ﴿those who disbelieve﴾, it is well known that what is meant is that they disbelieve in their Lord. It has been placed before its governing verb (ʿāmil) out of regard for the verse endings (fawāṣil), since when the endings come in harmony they are more pleasing to the ear and more agreeable to the soul. And He used ﴿thumma﴾ (then), which indicates delay; meaning that after they reflected, considered and knew, they disbelieved, we seek refuge in Allah, and ascribed equals to Him, making rivals for Him.

Among the benefits of this noble verse:

First: the praise of Allah for Himself. Indeed Allah praised Himself for creating the heavens and the earth. This is praise at the beginning of creation, that is, the creation of the heavens and the earth. There is another praise at the end, as in the last part of Surah az-Zumar, where Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying the praise of their Lord. And it will be judged between them with truth, and it will be said, "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ [az-Zumar 75]. (It is said): that is, all the worlds say it: "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

He also praised Himself for His transcendence above every defect and deficiency, and for His majesty and greatness, as He says: ﴿And say, "All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son and has not had a partner in dominion, nor has He any ally out of weakness; so magnify Him with [full] magnification."﴾ [al-Isra' 111]. He praised Himself, blessed and exalted, for sending down the Quran, saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has sent down to His Servant the Book and has not made therein any deviance. [He has made it] straight, to warn of severe punishment from Him﴾ [al-Kahf 1-2]. Allah praises Himself at great matters, because these great matters oblige the reflecting servant to praise Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for the perfection of His attributes and the perfection of His bounty and favour.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Creator of the heavens and the earth is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who created the heavens and the earth. No one has claimed that he creates the heavens and the earth, not even the polytheists; if they were asked, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would say, "Allah."

Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the heavens are created and not eternal, as shown by His saying: ﴿created the heavens and the earth﴾. In this there is a refutation of the philosophers who said that this world is eternal (qidam) and without beginning. Their view is rejected by the Book, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslims.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: that "heavens" is plural, because it is pluralized. And how many are they? Seven heavens, by the explicit text of the Quran.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the distinction in mentioning the heavens and the earth, where the heavens are mentioned in plural and the earth in singular. This is because the heavens are far greater than the earth, not in height, nor in extent, nor in anything else; everything in the heavens is greater than what is in the earth. Allah says: ﴿Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He constructed it. He raised its height and made it proportioned﴾ to the end [an-Nazi'at 27-28].

Among the benefits of this noble verse: a singular noun may be used to mean the genus, so it encompasses whatever exceeds the singular; as in His saying ﴿and the earth﴾.

Among the benefits of this noble verse, what may be derived from it: that whoever owns the surface of the earth owns what is beneath it, so it is not said that you have only one earth, and that you do not own the earth down to its depths. The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, have established this and said: the owner of the earth owns it down to the seventh earth. On this the hadith confirms, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever unjustly takes a span of land, Allah will collar him with it on the Day of Resurrection, from seven earths."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3198), and Muslim (1610 / 137), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl.]]

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the different expression between the creation of the heavens and the earth and the making of the darkness and the light. One may ask: why does the expression differ? Is it merely a difference of wording, or is there a real difference?

Let us consider: (ja'ala) comes with the meaning of (khalaqa) without doubt, and the proof for this is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate﴾ [an-Nisa' 1], and in another verse He says: ﴿It is He who created you from one soul and made from it its mate that he might dwell in tranquillity with her﴾ [al-A'raf 189]. This shows that (khalaqa) and (ja'ala) have one meaning, and on this basis the distinction here is merely a difference of wording.

It was also said that there is a difference between them: creation (khalq) is the bringing into being of the essence of the created thing and its origin, whereas darkness is an attribute of the created thing, and likewise light. For this reason you never find for light a body that is seen. Look at light: it only appears on a surface; in open space light does not appear. What we sometimes see as a white beam when we strike something with penetrating force against light is not the light itself, but a reflection of small particles in the air; it is not the light but a reflection of it. Since light and darkness are not perceptible things, but appear in other things, He expressed them with the word (ja'ala). Without doubt this is more eloquent than saying there is no difference between them and that only the wording differs.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the combination of plural "darknesses" and singular "light". Some said: light is singular because it is one thing; light is light, whereas darknesses are plural because they differ according to the body that produces the darkness. For example, if you have a waxed glass and place it between the bulb and the ground, is there darkness or not?

Students: Yes.

The Shaykh: But it is faint. If you place something thick, it becomes clear black darkness. Therefore darknesses are pluralized, because darkness varies according to the body that produces it or in which it occurs.

Others said: because darknesses are the original state and light is an addition to them, and darknesses are known to vary. For example, the darkness at a time when the sky is covered with clouds is not like when the sky is clear; the darkness at the bottom of the sea is not like the darkness at its surface, and so on. This is if we say that what is meant by darknesses and light is what is perceptible of them. But if we say, and this is the correct view as we have established, that it includes perceptible and non-perceptible darkness, and likewise perceptible and non-perceptible light, then the matter is clear, because the branches of disbelief are many while faith is one thing; its branches are merely branches, while its root is fixed. Indeed, the path of Allah, the Exalted, is one, while the other roads are many. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And that this is My path, [which is] straight, so follow it. And do not follow [other] ways, for they will separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 153].

Among the benefits of this verse: the folly of the disbelievers, and that they lack sound intellect. Its meaning: after these great signs became manifest, they ascribed equals to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; they made Him equals and rivals. This shows their folly, even if they are clever. This is supported by the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself﴾ [al-Baqarah 130]; and by the fact that Allah always reproaches the disbelievers for lacking intellect, most of them do not reason, and the verses on this are many. This is the truth: that the disbelievers are not intelligent, and the negation of intellect here means the negation of intellect of conduct. What is the intellect of perception? They are intelligent in terms of perception, which is why the acts of worship are binding upon them and Islam is binding upon them, but they are not intelligent in terms of conduct; rather they are foolish. How excellent is what Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said about the theologians (mutakallimun): he said, they were given understandings but not knowledge, and given cleverness but not purification (zaka'). They have understanding, but they do not have knowledge, meaning knowledge of the Sharia, and they have perception, but they do not have intellect.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the lordship (rububiyyah) of Allah is general to both believer and disbeliever; this is shown by His saying: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve in their Lord ascribe equals﴾, where He made Himself Lord of these people. There is no difficulty in this. But this is the general lordship; there is a special lordship for the believers which entails protection, care, preservation and nurture. Both kinds came together in the words of Pharaoh's magicians: ﴿We believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ [al-A'raf 121-122]. The first is general, and the second is specific.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿It is He who created you from clay﴾ [al-An'am 2]. When He mentioned the creation of the heavens and the earth, He followed it with the creation of us, so He said: ﴿It is He who created you from clay﴾. Clay (ṭīn) is earth moistened with water, or mixed with water, and it is well known. This refers to the creation of our origin, who is Adam. As for the human being, he was created from a despised fluid, from the sperm-drop (nuṭfah). But Adam was created from clay.

﴿Then He decreed a term﴾ [al-An'am 2]: that is, He determined a term which will end and come to its close.

﴿And there is a named term with Him﴾ [al-An'am 2]. ﴿Named (musammā)﴾ means known to Allah. Here, the better course is to pause at ﴿Then He decreed a term﴾ and not to continue, because continuing may give the impression of contradiction. Its explanation is that the first, ﴿decreed a term﴾, is in the accusative, while the second is in the nominative, and the ruling also differs, as will become clear, Allah willing, in the benefits (al-fawā'id).

﴿And there is a named term with Him﴾ with Allah. It is the Hour (qiyām al-sā'ah), for this is among the things specific to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They ask you about the Hour. Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 63], and He the Exalted said: ﴿They ask you about the Hour, when will be its appointed time? Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'rāf 187]. This is with Allah; no one knows it, and no one knows when it will end. As for the first term, we know its ending when we find that a man whom Allah brought into being then caused to die; the term has ended, or not?

Allah decreed his term and we know it. But the named term, known to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, is specific to Allah in its knowledge.

﴿Then﴾, that is: after you have learned that you were created from clay, and that terms end with knowledge from you, and there is another term, not known, after this ﴿you doubt﴾. ﴿Doubting (imtirā')﴾ is doubt, that is, you doubt in the resurrection. So consider now how He mentioned in the earlier verses the polytheism of these people toward their Lord, meaning the disbelievers, and then mentioned another kind, which is disbelief in the Last Day, for doubt concerning what requires certainty is disbelief.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the children of Adam are created, having not existed before. From where is this taken?

From His saying: ﴿It is He who created﴾ [al-Baqarah 29]. And Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has said: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ [al-Insān 1]. ﴿Has (hal)﴾ here means (qad). Whoever is twenty years old, before that he was twenty-one years ago, yes, he was not a thing worth mentioning, then Allah brought him into existence. In this is evidence that the children of Adam are originated and were created from nothing.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the indication to the origin of the children of Adam, that they are from clay. And clay is from where? From the earth. And Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out a second time﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 55].

If someone says: what is the reconciliation between this verse and the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And We created man from clay of sounding dry earth﴾ [al-Ḥijr 26], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He created you from dust﴾ [al-Rūm 20]?

The reconciliation between them is easy. The origin of the children of Adam is dust, on which water was poured, and it became clay (ṭīn). It remained for a long period of time and became ṣalṣāl (dried clay that rings), because it turns black; and when something is made from it, it becomes ṣalṣāl that has a sound. If you strike it with your finger, it has a sound. So there is no disagreement and no contradiction.

Know that a contradiction can never occur between two definitive (qaṭ'ī) proofs, for if a conflict were found between them, neither would be definitive; because the definitive is that its opposite is impossible. So a conflict between two definitive proofs is never possible: not in the Qur'an, nor in the Sunnah, nor between the Qur'an and the Sunnah, nor between rational and transmitted proofs. This is impossible, for if we supposed it, one of them would certainly be incorrect; since the relation between two definitive proofs is contradiction, and two contradictories, what? They cannot coexist nor be absent together; one of them must exist, and they cannot both be combined, nor agree.

So when a conflict between two definitive proofs appears to you, know that the error is in your understanding, and that it is possible to reconcile them. Or one of them is not definitive, and the ruling goes to what? To the definitive one. But if both are speculative (ẓannī), then conflict is possible, and at that point one looks to preference (tarjīḥ).

If the Qur'an contains what outwardly appears to conflict in a definitive way, know that this is what? It is impossible, ever. Either the indication is not definitive, or the ruling is abrogated (mansūkh). But that the ruling and the indication remain definitive in two verses, for example, that is impossible.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the ruling belongs to Allah the Mighty and Majestic alone, by His saying: ﴿He decreed a term, and there is a named term with Him﴾, and none can change these terms.

* Among its benefits: that whoever dies by being killed has died at his appointed term which Allah decreed for him; for Allah decreed it. It cannot be said: had he not been killed, he would not have died. This is impossible, for Allah decreed that he die by killing; so he is killed at a term.

If someone says: had this man not been killed, say at twelve noon, he could have had lunch at one o'clock. What do we say?

We say: that is impossible, because Allah decreed it thus, so it must occur. Every dead person dies by what? By his decreed term, neither advancing nor delaying. But the means may advance or delay according to a person's view.

Likewise, long life through maintaining family ties is also decreed. We cannot say: if this one were disobedient, he would have died before his death... if he were keeping ties? Why? Because we said: Allah decreed that he be one who keeps ties, and that his life be prolonged. Allah decreed a term, and it cannot be delayed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the known term, which is the Hour, is with Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and no one can reach knowledge of it. This is an agreed matter among the Muslims. Even the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about it by Jibril, and Jibril is the best of the angels, and Muhammad is the best of mankind, and he asked him about the Hour, and he said: "The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah.] So if these two noble messengers do not know when the Hour is, then whoever is below them is more so.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rebuke of folly and heedlessness toward those people who know their origin and source, yet they doubt and are uncertain about the named term with Allah, which is the Day of Resurrection.

In Surah al-Jāthiyah, those who deny resurrection argued: ﴿They said: Bring our fathers, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Jāthiyah 25]. So what do you say about this claim?

It is not correct, because those who informed of the Resurrection did not say: they will be raised now. The time has not yet come. But this is a kind of analogy aimed at misleading the creation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 6, verse 3:

Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth; He knows what you conceal and what you disclose, and He knows what you earn.﴾ [al-An'am 3].

His words: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens﴾. ﴿Allah﴾ is a proper name (ʿalam) for the Lord, mighty and majestic, which belongs to no other, and this is agreed upon among the Muslims.

Is it a derived name (mushtaqq) or not? It is derived from the divinity (al-ulūhiyyah), and its origin is (al-Ilāh). Know that all the names of Allah are derived, as is evident; there is never in them a rigid (jāmid) name for Allah, mighty and majestic.

His words: ﴿in the heavens﴾ are connected to the name, because we have just told you that this name is derived, and a derived noun may take a complement, as the author of the rules of sentence structure (Qawā'id al-Jumal) said:

"The preposition must be linked to a verb or its meaning, like 'murtaqī' (one who ascends)."

Therefore ﴿in the heavens﴾ is connected to the word Allah, since it is derived, and a derived noun may take a prepositional phrase. But what is the meaning of ﴿in the heavens﴾?

The meaning is that He is over the heavens, and it is not intended that He is within them while they encompass Him, for that is impossible; Allah, Exalted is He, is greater than everything. Or we may say: the intended meaning is not the essence; the meaning is that He is worshipped (ma'lūh) in the heavens, that the people of the heavens worship Him.

His words: ﴿and on the earth﴾: the "wa" is a conjunction particle, and ﴿the earth﴾ is conjoined to ﴿the heavens﴾, so the meaning is: Allah is in the heavens and on the earth; i.e., worshipped in what? In the heavens and on the earth. This verse is then like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf 84].

On this interpretation there is no difficulty: Allah is God in the heavens and also on the earth.

Some scholars held that the verse has a pause (waqf) after ﴿the heavens﴾, and this is based on making Allah a proper name for the Essence rather than for the one who is worshipped by His servants; that is, the meaning is that Allah is in the heavens, like His saying: ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven?﴾ [al-Mulk 16].

Then He resumed and said: ﴿and on the earth He knows your secret and your open speech﴾, so ﴿on the earth﴾ is connected to what follows, namely His saying: ﴿He knows your secret and your open speech﴾. As for the first reading, the meaning of the verse is clear: Allah is worshipped in the heavens and worshipped on the earth; just as He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, He is worshipped in the heavens and the earth, and by this is meant the affirmation of divinity in the heavens and the earth just as lordship (rubūbiyyah) is affirmed. Creation is among the requirements of lordship. There is no difficulty in this.

The connection (munāsabah) according to the second view is that the meaning is that Allah's Essence, not someone who worships Him, is in the heavens. The connection is that His being in the heavens, despite their vast distance, does not prevent His knowledge of you while you are on the earth. He is in the heavens, and yet on the earth He knows your secret and your open speech. Have you understood the difference between the two meanings?

The first meaning, that Allah is in the heavens and on the earth, means that His divinity is established in the heavens and on the earth; i.e., those in the heavens worship Him and those on the earth worship Him. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf 84].

The second meaning says: Allah Himself is in the heavens, i.e., above them, and yet He knows your secret and open speech on the earth; so His distance is no obstacle to His knowledge of what is secret and open among you on the earth.

Thus the second meaning contains no mention of divinity, but it does contain mention of encompassing knowledge, Allah's encompassing of us, mighty and majestic, even though He is in the heavens.

This is explained by the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has heard the speech of she who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah, and Allah hears your mutual discourse﴾ [al-Mujadilah 1]. Where did the discourse take place?

On the earth, while Allah, Exalted is He, is in the heaven. So this verse is like an explanation of His saying: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth; He knows your secret and your open speech.﴾

His words: ﴿He knows your secret﴾ means: what is in the breasts. Secret speech is of two kinds: secrecy within the self, and secrecy with another. For example, when a person speaks to himself about something, this is secrecy with the self; and when he tells another a secret that the one beside him does not hear, this is secrecy with another. This is why we call the recitation in the noon and afternoon prayers, for instance, "silent" (sirriyyah), even though a person pronounces it and hears himself; yet we still call it secret. And we call what a person says to himself "secret" too. So "secret" includes both meanings: He knows what is concealed in our souls and what we do not show to anyone, and what we tell others in a hidden manner that others do not hear.

﴿and your open speech﴾ means: what you speak aloud and make public.

﴿and He knows what you earn﴾ means: He knows your earnings, of good and evil, of religion and worldly life, of knowledge and other things; everything that occurs, Allah knows it, mighty and majestic; nothing is hidden from Him. We ask Allah to deal with us by His pardon.

* Student: As is said, those who claim that Allah is present in every place cite verses like this one, and His saying: ﴿There is no secret conference of three but that He is their fourth, nor of five but that He is their sixth﴾ [al-Mujadilah 7], and the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating" [Muslim (482/215) from Abu Hurayrah]. With such evidences they say that Allah is in every place. How do we respond to them?

* Shaykh: Yes, we respond to them with complete ease. First, we say: you have now followed the ambiguous (mutashābih), meaning that the verses have a possibility of what they claim, so it is ambiguous; and you have left the clear verses (muhkamāt) affirming that Allah, Exalted is He, is distinct from His creation, above His creation; you have left them, so you are of the second category: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that of it which is ambiguous﴾ [Al 'Imran 7]. So if they cite this verse, we say: it is like a person's saying, "So-and-so is the governor of Makkah and Madinah," meaning his authority is established in Makkah and Madinah, and it does not mean that he himself is in Makkah and Madinah, for that is impossible. Is that not so?

So Allah's divinity is in the heavens and on the earth, and He is not in the heavens nor on the earth. Is that complete?

As for accompaniment (ma'iyyah), we say that it does not contradict elevation (uluww), even among created things; in Arabic they say, "We kept traveling and the moon was with us," or "we kept traveling and the Pole Star was with us," and this is a common, acceptable expression. So the meaning of "Allah is with us" is that He is watching over us, though He is above. If it is possible for elevation and accompaniment to coexist in the case of a creature, their coexistence in the case of the Creator is all the more fitting.

* Student: Allah is present in all existence; the matter is (...).

* Shaykh: In all existence? It is forbidden. First, because Allah being in all existence is not correct, unless they mean by "existence" the sense of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), so that Allah is "existing in every existent," which is exactly the doctrine of the Hulūliyyah (incarnationists).

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, how do we respond to the Sufis who say: if you say that Allah, mighty and majestic, is established upon the Throne, then where was He before that? (...) on the earth?

* Shaykh: No. The Companions asked the Messenger, and he said: "He was in 'ama'," and 'ama' means a thin cloud; it is a light cloud.

* Student: In the sky, meaning?

* Shaykh: In the sky. All of these who are driven to this are those who thought that the Lord, mighty and majestic, is encompassed by creatures and is like a human being. But if they measured Allah with His true measure, and knew that the Lord, mighty and majestic, is greater than everything, and that no one can imagine Him, then... This is why some scholars said a fine phrase: "Reflect upon the signs of Allah, and do not reflect upon the Essence of Allah."

* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth; He knows your secret and your open speech and He knows what you earn (3). And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord but that they turn away from it (4). They have certainly denied the truth when it came to them; so the news of that which they used to mock will soon reach them (5). Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth as We have not established you, and We sent the sky upon them in abundant rain and made rivers flow beneath them; then We destroyed them for their sins and produced after them other generations﴾ [al-An'am 3–6].
* Shaykh: Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿He it is who created you from clay﴾. What is the reconciliation between this noble verse and His saying: ﴿So let man observe from what he was created. He was created from a fluid, ejected﴾ [al-Tariq 5, 6]?

* Student: We said: Adam was created from clay.

* Shaykh: From ejected fluid; this is in terms of the origin: clay in terms of the origin, and this in terms of the branch that proceeds from the origin.

What is the reconciliation between His saying here, blessed and exalted: ﴿from clay﴾ and His saying in another verse: ﴿from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran 59]?

* Student: That when water is poured on dust it becomes ṣalṣāl.

* Shaykh: It becomes clay.

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Meaning that dust is the origin; when water is poured on it, it becomes clay, and when it remains for a period it becomes ṣalṣāl.

Can there be a contradiction between two verses that are definitive in their indication? Answer.

* Student: It is not possible.

* Shaykh: What is it that is not possible?

* Student: A contradiction between two verses definitive in indication is not possible.

* Shaykh: Why not?

* Student: Because if a contradiction between two definitive verses occurred, it would be a contradiction among the rulings from Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and this does not happen.

* Shaykh: It would be a combination of opposites, and that is impossible. Now, if such a thing occurred to a person, i.e., he thought there was a contradiction between two definitive verses?

* Student: It would be a deficiency in his understanding.

* Shaykh: Yes, we say: this is evidence of the deficiency of his understanding or knowledge, so he should return again to reflection until it becomes clear to him that there is no contradiction; for Allah said: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisa 82].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the divinity of Allah is established in the heavens and the earth; those in the heavens and those on the earth worship Him; from His saying: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, blessed and exalted, knows the secret and the open; He knows what a person conceals and what he discloses. Secrecy may be secrecy within the self, and may be secrecy with another in a specific manner; and disclosure is the open declaration that is not hidden. So Allah knows the secret, whether with oneself or with another in a specific manner, or the open.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the comprehensiveness of the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted; for His saying "your secret" includes everyone, and Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah, there is no deity but Him; He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha 98], and verses with this meaning are many.

* Among them: what follows from our belief that Allah knows the secret and the open. Believing this requires that we not oppose the command of Allah, mighty and majestic, by abandoning an obligation or committing a sin, because we know that Allah, Exalted is He, knows it; and if knowledge did not bear this noble fruit, our knowledge would be of no benefit.

Pay attention to this matter: many people do not care about the behavioral benefits that follow from the names and attributes of Allah, and this is something indispensable; this is the fruit. When you know that Allah knows your secret and your open speech, you feel shame before Him, so you do not abandon what is obligatory, nor do you do what is forbidden.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted, of what one earns; i.e., of the deeds a person acquires, whether it is worldly earning or otherworldly earning, for Allah, Exalted is He, knows it, and nothing is hidden from Him. This benefit entails that we not earn anything that Allah has forbidden us.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And there does not come to them any sign from among the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.﴾ [Al-An'am 4] (ma) is a negation particle.

As for His saying ﴿min āyah﴾ (from any sign), the ﴿min﴾ (from) is grammatically superfluous (ziyadah i'rāban) but not superfluous in meaning, because it has a meaning, which is emphasis of the negation. It converts a negation that may be general or specific into one that is general, so it turns the negated sentence into a clear statement of generality, like the particle "lā" of genus (lā al-nāfiyah li-l-jins), which is explicit in generality.

How do we parse it if we say that ﴿min﴾ is grammatically superfluous?

We say: ﴿min﴾ is a superfluous preposition (ḥarf jarr zā'id i'rāban), and ﴿āyah﴾ is the subject (fā'il) of "ta'tī," in the nominative case, marked by a presumed ḍammah at its end, which could not appear because the position was occupied by the movement of the superfluous particle. An example of this is the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Lest you should say, "There came to us no bearer of good tidings and no warner"﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 19]. Here ﴿min﴾ is grammatically superfluous, and ﴿bashīr﴾ is the subject, nominative, marked by a presumed ḍammah at its end, which could not appear because the position was occupied by the movement of the superfluous preposition.

As for His saying ﴿min āyah﴾: the āyah (sign) is the indication (al-'alāmah), but it is more specific than the general indication, because it is definitive in showing [the truth]. A 'alāmah may be less than that, but an āyah is explicit that it is an indication of that for which it came. The signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are divided into two types: kawniyyah (cosmic) and shar'iyyah (legislative), as will come, God willing, in the benefits.

﴿min āyāti rabbihim﴾: the ﴿min﴾ here indicates the genus (li-bayān al-jins) and is not like the first one. It is for specifying the genus, due to His saying ﴿min āyah﴾, because a sign may be from Allah and may be from other than Him, but "from the signs of their Lord" [specifies that they are from Him].

As for His saying ﴿rabbihim﴾, it means their Creator, their Owner, and their Manager, because lordship (rubūbiyyah) includes these three meanings: creator, owner, and manager. This is what lordship requires.

﴿illā kānū ʿanhā muʿriḍīn﴾: this ﴿illā﴾ is an affirmation of the negation; that is, "there does not come to them except that they turn away from it," turning away from reflecting upon it and from what it indicates, so it is as if they had not seen the signs. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe, even if every sign should come to them until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus 96–97]. So, turning away from them, is it with their faces or with their hearts?

All of it; it includes both this and that. It may be said to him, "Come and look at the sign of Allah," and he turns away and does not look; or he may see it, but turn away from contemplating it in the heart, because he is—and we seek refuge in Allah—veiled from good, so he does not wish for it to reach him.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the arrogance of these deniers. The reason is that no sign comes to them except that they turn away from it. The Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ for a sign, so he showed them the splitting of the moon; he pointed to the moon and it split into two parts.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3636) and Muslim (2800/44) from the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud.]] The people witnessed it, and Allah referred to it in His saying: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ [Al-Qamar 1]. It was a perceptible splitting, and by "the moon" is meant the visible, well-known moon.

The philosophers and astronomers denied that the moon split, and said: "It is impossible, because disintegration cannot occur in the celestial bodies." So shall we accept their statement and reject the authentic, well-known, widely transmitted hadiths, or reject their statement?

* The students: The second.

* The Shaykh: The obligation upon the believer is the second: to reject every statement that contradicts the Book and the Sunnah, whoever its speaker may be. How can we say it is impossible for the celestial bodies to change, when the one who changes them is—who? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, their Creator, who does whatever He wills. It was a perceptible splitting of the perceptible moon, not as the astronomers said. They distorted the Book and the Sunnah on its account, and said that the reports of the splitting are solitary reports (akhbār aḥādiyyah) that admit of interpretation or rejection, and that as for the Qur'an, "the moon split" means that the light of prophethood became manifest. This is an error; it is not correct.

If someone says: "The Quraysh saw this sign, and Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has decreed that whoever is given the sign they ask for and does not believe, He destroys. So why did Allah not destroy the Quraysh?"

* A student: They did not ask for that specific sign.

* The Shaykh: Yes. The answer to this is that those who are destroyed are those who ask for a specific sign; when it comes and they disbelieve in it, Allah destroys them, because they are then defiant toward Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for those who ask for a general sign, which is then specified by Allah, these are not destroyed.

It may also bear another meaning: we may say that this generality may be specified, so Allah, Glorified and Exalted, did not destroy them, because the matter is as the Prophet ﷺ said when the angel of the mountains came to him and said: "If you wish, I will bring the two Akhshabs down upon them," and they are the two great mountains surrounding Makkah. But the Prophet ﷺ said: "No, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins those who worship Allah and do not associate anything with Him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3231) and Muslim (1795/111) from the hadith of ʿAisha.]] The non-destruction of the Quraysh is because of what Allah, Majestic and Exalted, knows: that from their loins will come those sincere to Allah and those who strive in the way of Allah. Did this occur or not?

* Students: It occurred.

* The Shaykh: It occurred without doubt. So either the answer is as the brother said, or the answer is what we have mentioned.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is Wise and Merciful. This is because He brings signs to the creation, and this is clear wisdom, for it is not reasonable for a man to come and tell the people that he is a messenger, and to make lawful the blood, wealth, offspring and women of those who do not believe in him, without there being a sign that proves his truthfulness. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no prophet"—meaning whom Allah sent—"except that he was given signs such that people believed in the like of them."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4981) and Muslim (152/239) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] It is necessary; this is from the aspect of wisdom.

From the aspect of mercy: Allah has shown mercy to the creation by, when He sends messengers to them, giving them signs that indicate their truthfulness. Had He willed, He could have sent messengers without signs and then seized whoever denied them; but His wisdom and mercy refuse to send messengers without a sign.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of lordship for the disbelievers, because of His saying ﴿min āyāti rabbihim﴾. This is general lordship. The lordship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is divided into general and specific: His lordship over His friends is specific, and over His friends and enemies alike is general. Correspondingly, worship is divided into what? General and specific. The general is like His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93], and the specific is like His saying: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from among Our servants﴾ [Fatir 32], and His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [Al-Furqan 1]. The examples are many.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the danger of turning away from the signs, and that one who turns away from the signs is feared not to be guided to them, because of His saying: ﴿except that they turn away from it.﴾

This is supported by—that is, by the danger of turning away from the signs—the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight, as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [Al-An'am 110]. The kaf here is for causation: ﴿as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾. This is indeed a serious matter. The student of knowledge must keep it before his eyes. If he is walking along a particular path and texts come that contradict it, some people may hesitate and try to distort the texts that oppose their path, and this is a great danger. Rather, it is obligatory for the believer to submit to the texts from the moment they reach him, as the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, used to do: as soon as the Messenger commanded something, they did it, and as soon as he forbade something, they abandoned it. So a person's hesitation at the very first arrival of the truth is a great danger. The verse is clear in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [Al-An'am 110]. And Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿But if they turn away, know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins. And indeed, many of the people are defiant.﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 49]

Allah, blessed and exalted, then says:

﴿So they have indeed denied the truth when it came to them, but there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.﴾ [Al-An'am 5].

﴿So they have indeed denied the truth﴾: The fa' is conjunctive (ʿāṭifah), and qad indicates certainty (taḥqīq). With the past tense verb, qad most often indicates certainty; with the present tense verb, it most often indicates diminution (taqlīl), as in their saying: "the miser may be generous (qad yajūd al-bakhīl), and the liar may speak the truth (qad yasduq al-kādhib)." However, it may also come for emphasis even with the present tense, and from this is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Allah certainly knows those among you who hinder others, and those who say to their brothers, "Come to us"﴾ [Al-Ahzab 18]. Here qad is, without doubt, for emphasis, but it also indicates continuity; that is, this knowledge applies in the present and the future.

His saying here: "qad kadhdhabū" (they have denied) is for certainty.

﴿they denied the truth when it came to them﴾: The truth (al-ḥaqq) is what the messengers, upon them be peace, brought, all of which is true because it is from Allah. Truth is that which is firmly established: if it is a report, then by its occurrence, and if it is a ruling, then by its being established. Its opposite is falsehood (al-bāṭil); in reports, falsehood is lying, and in rulings, falsehood is what opposes the Shari'ah. Here, "they denied the truth when it came to them": we say the truth is what the messengers brought, of true reports and just rulings.

﴿when it came to them﴾: Lamma here means "when" (ḥīn), that is, "when it came to them." You should know that lammā has several meanings: it comes in the sense of "when," making it temporal, as in the verse; it comes as a conditional particle, sharing with (in) the function of a condition, as in Allah's saying: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Indeed, this is clear magic"﴾ [Yunus 76], where it is conditional; it comes in the sense of (illā) "except," as in Allah's saying: ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾ [At-Tariq 4], meaning "except that over it is a guardian"; and it comes as a negation that jazms (apocopates) the present-tense verb, as in Allah's saying: ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 8], in the sense of lam. However, lammā differs from lam in that it indicates the proximity of what follows it; lam is an absolute negation. You may say: "Fulan lam yaqum" (Fulan did not stand up), which is an absolute negation, and "Lammā yaqum Fulan" (Fulan has not yet stood up), a negation meaning that until now he has not stood, but he will stand up soon.

In the noble verse we are reading now: ﴿lammā jāʾahum﴾, how do we parse it?

It is an adverb of time in the sense of "when" (ḥīn), and in this case it is indeclinable (mabniyy), because it is in reality a particle (ḥarf), not merely resembling one. The basis of indeclinability, as you have known, is the resemblance of a noun to a particle, but this itself is a particle; so it is an adverb, but built on sukūn in a position of naṣb, in the sense of "when" (ḥīn).

﴿So they have indeed denied the truth when it came to them, but there will come﴾: The fa' is conjunctive, and it may also be causal. ﴿there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾: That is, there will come to them the thing they were told of, the news (al-anbāʾ) had reached them before, but what is meant is that there will come to them the punishment of the news they used to mock.

﴿the news of that which they used to mock﴾: That is, they take it as a jest, play and laughter. As we all know, the disbelievers take religion as a jest, and they also take the people of religion as a jest, do they not?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say, "Was it Allah and His verses and His messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ [At-Tawbah 65], and He, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed. And when they passed by them, they exchanged winks. And when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 29–31].

So His saying ﴿that which they used to mock﴾ includes their mockery of religion, their mockery of the messengers and their followers, and even of Allah, mighty and majestic; they will find this out. Let us return to the benefits.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these people, despite the verses being continually sent to them, denied the truth and did not respond to it. Denying the truth after it has come is worse than denying it before it came, such that a person hears about it but it is not confirmed; for one to whom the truth has come and who denies it, his denial is greater.

* Another benefit of this noble verse: this ruling applies to those upon whom the proof has been established by the coming of the truth to them. As for one who does not know the truth, he falls into two categories: sometimes he adheres to the religion of truth without knowing it, and sometimes he adheres to the religion of falsehood and does not ascribe himself to the religion of truth.

The first: one who adheres to falsehood but ascribes himself to the religion of truth, so he prays, pays zakat, fasts, and performs Hajj, but he seeks help from the dead. We say: we do not judge his Islam invalid if the proof has not been established against him.

The second: one who does not adhere to the religion of Islam at all; the proof has not reached him and he does not know that he is astray, but he adheres to a religion other than Islam. How do we treat him?

We treat him as a disbeliever. Therefore, if someone now dies who has not been reached by the call, from among non-Muslims, we do not pray over him nor ask mercy for him, because he adhered to a religion other than Islam; but his affair in the Hereafter is up to Allah, mighty and majestic. As for one who is a Muslim adhering to the religion of Islam, who says, "I testify that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the messenger of Allah," establishes prayer and gives zakat, but commits major shirk without knowing it is major shirk, we treat him in the manner of a Muslim: we wash him, shroud him, pray over him, and bury him among us, so long as the proof has not been established against him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that these people will be given respite, and the punishment will not come to them immediately, due to His saying: ﴿but there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾.

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿So they have indeed denied the truth when it came to them, but there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾, which we have explained.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these people denied the truth after it had come to them, so their denial is more reprehensible and their sin greater, due to the establishment of the proof against them.

* Among its benefits: a warning to these people of punishment, due to His saying: ﴿but there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the denial of these people is accompanied by mockery, for they scoff: "How will we be resurrected when we have been bones and crumbled dust?!" and they say: ﴿Has he made the gods into one god? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing﴾ [Sad 5]. So there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these disbelievers have obstinacy, we seek refuge in Allah; for they combined their disbelief with mockery, so neither the Shari'ah nor the one who brought it was spared from their ridicule.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ The interrogative here enters upon a negation. The interrogative particle (alif of interrogation, with "lam" and "ma" forming "a-lam") enters upon a negative, and when the interrogative hamza enters upon a negation, its meaning becomes taqrir (affirmation, confirming a fact by way of a question). This is as in His saying: ﴿Does not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted﴾ [al-Mulk 14], and as in His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1]; meaning, "We have indeed expanded for you your breast," and "Does not He who created know," meaning, "He who created does know." So when the negative particle follows the interrogative hamza, it is for taqrir.

His saying: ﴿they have seen﴾ may mean the seeing here is knowledge-based seeing (ru'yah 'ilmiyyah), or sight-based seeing (ru'yah basariyyah). The lands through which they passed, their ruin is seen by what? By sight, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning (137) and at night﴾ [al-Saffat 137-138]. And the lands they did not pass through, their seeing is knowledge-based, transmitted by those who relate reports.

His saying: ﴿how many We destroyed﴾ means: We caused to perish. And ﴿how many﴾ here is for multiplicity; meaning, nations which We destroyed.

﴿from before them of generations﴾. Qarn (generation): some of the scholars defined it as a hundred years, or forty years, and some defined it saying: the intended meaning of qarn is the people who perish, for example, within the span of seventy years, as these present ones perish and others succeed them. They supported this with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best of people is my generation (qarni), then those who follow them"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2652) and Muslim (2533 / 212), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]], his generation being the Companions, and within roughly a hundred years they perished.

﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, We had established them on the earth﴾. His saying: ﴿We had established them﴾, the pronoun refers to qarn considered as a collective noun; i.e., We established these generations on the earth.

﴿such as We have not established for you﴾ means: We gave them what they could use to gain strength, and by which they secured what We have not established for you, rather greater and greater, and the earlier ones were stronger than the later ones, and had more wealth and children, and cultivated the earth more than they cultivated it.

His saying: ﴿such as We have not established for you﴾ contains a shift (iltifat) from the third person to what? Complete it?

* Student: To the second person.

* Shaykh: Yes, to the second person, which is address to the present; the iltifat occurs from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (hudur), and from the second to the third, and from explicit noun to pronoun. There are various kinds, and its benefit is to alert the listener or reader to what comes afterward. The reason for this: when speech is in one uniform tone, a person flows along with it, but when it changes, he pauses. What is it that has occurred? So this iltifat serves to alert whom? The reader and listener, and it is one of the styles of the Arabic language, and the Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language: ﴿And We sent down the sky upon them in abundant rain﴾.

Or the reader to what comes afterward. The reason: when speech is in one uniform tone, a person flows along with it, but when it changes he pauses. What has occurred? So this iltifat alerts whom? The reader and listener, and it is one of the styles of the Arabic language, and the Qur'an was revealed in Arabic.

﴿And We sent down the sky upon them in abundant rain﴾ [al-An'am 6]. The intended meaning of "sky" here is rain, and it is expressed as "sky" because it descends from the sky. ﴿Abundant (midrar)﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from ﴿sky﴾, meaning: while it was pouring abundantly upon them; whenever their land needed water, the water descended.

﴿And We made the rivers flow beneath them﴾. ﴿The rivers﴾ may be the rivers of snow melt that seep from mountain peaks, or it may be the valleys formed by rain. Whether it is this or that, there is no doubt the land would be fertile, and their livestock and they themselves would eat from it.

﴿So We destroyed them for their sins﴾. ﴿We destroyed them﴾: We caused them to perish. ﴿For their sins﴾: the particle (ba') here indicates causation, i.e., because of their sins; and sins means acts of disobedience.

﴿And We produced after them another generation﴾. ﴿We produced﴾ means: We created anew, after them, another people. Did the later people disobey or obey? Some disobeyed and some obeyed, but Allah said: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession. Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him, so We made them follow one another and made them into tales﴾ [al-Mu'minun 44].

* In this noble verse: a warning to those who deny the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that what befell the earlier nations may befall them. The reason: Allah established that they had seen the nations destroyed before.

* Among its benefits: inference from the greater to the lesser. The reason: since they were stronger than those, Allah sent down abundant rain upon them and made rivers flow beneath them, and yet He destroyed them; so those below them are more deserving of destruction.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: demonstrating the greatness and jealousy (ghayrah) of Allah the Glorified, in that He destroyed those people despite their strength and blessings.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that whatever blessings are obtained and whatever calamities are averted come from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, due to His saying: ﴿We had established them on the earth﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirming causes, due to His saying: ﴿We destroyed them for their sins﴾.

* Among its benefits: that sins are causes of destruction. But is the intended destruction physical, i.e., that people die, or lose their wealth, or the like, or does it include both physical and spiritual destruction, which is the death of hearts?

* Student: Both.

* Shaykh: Both; it includes this and that. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If they turn away, then know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins﴾ [al-Ma'idah 49], making their turning away a cause of sins.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the completeness of the power and dominion of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, in that He destroys peoples and produces others; because the command is His, the kingdom is His, and the dominion is His, so He does what He wills of destruction and creation.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said, explaining the arrogance of these people who denied the Messenger (ﷺ), saying: ﴿And even if We had sent down to you a written scripture on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieve would have said, "This is not but obvious magic."﴾ [Al-An'am 7]. The "law" (law) here is conditional, as shown by the presence of a protasis and an apodosis. Where is the protasis? ﴿We had sent down﴾, and the apodosis is ﴿those who disbelieve would have said﴾.

﴿And even if We had sent down to you﴾: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿a written scripture on paper﴾: meaning, an ordinary writing that people can perceive.

﴿and they had touched it with their hands﴾: meaning, they did not imagine it from a distance, but it was right before them, touching it as it descended from the sky to the Messenger (ﷺ).

As for His saying ﴿touched it with their hands﴾: if someone asks, "Is there touching other than with the hand?" The answer: if you wish, say yes, because a person touches with his foot, touches with his tongue, and touches with all parts of his skin. And if you wish, say that touching is done with the hand, but the hand is mentioned here for emphasis, like His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [Al-An'am 38], and it is well known that a bird flies only with a wing.

﴿those who disbelieve would have said﴾: this is the answer. ﴿Those who disbelieve would have said, "This is not but obvious magic"﴾: here the noun is put in place of the pronoun. Where is it? ﴿Those who disbelieve would have said﴾, and He did not say "they would have said," indicating two things:

The first thing: recording these people as disbelievers, meaning passing a ruling that they are disbelievers.

The second: that whoever says the same as their saying is a disbeliever.

So there are two benefits: a transitive benefit and an inherent benefit. The inherent benefit is the ruling that they are disbelievers, and the transitive benefit is that whoever says their saying is a disbeliever.

﴿Those who disbelieve would have said, "This is not but obvious magic"﴾: the (in) here is negative, as shown by His saying ﴿but﴾, and when (illa, "but") follows it, it is for negation, and it may be for negation even if (illa) does not follow it, but when (illa) follows it, it is for negation.

(In) comes as negative, as here, and comes as conditional, like: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾ [Az-Zumar 7].

And it comes as a lightened form of the heavy (inna), like His saying: ﴿Indeed, these two are but sorcerers﴾ [Ta-Ha 63]; because the original of ﴿in hadhani la-sahirani﴾ is (inna hadhani la-sahirani).

And it comes as superfluous, as in the words of the poet:

"Banu Ghudanah, you are not gold..." ∗∗∗ ......................
And the estimation is: "you are not gold," but it came superfluously. This is not strange; this shows that the Arabic language is broad, contrary to those who say it is narrow because its meanings are more than its words. We say: that a single letter or a single word comes with multiple meanings shows the flexibility of the Arabic language, not the scarcity of its uses, and there is no doubt that when a language is flexible, it is broader for those who speak it and easier for them.

﴿This﴾: the referent is the scripture on the paper.

﴿Is not but obvious magic﴾: Magic (sihr): everything hidden is called magic, derived from as-sahar, which is the last part of the night, and it is generally hidden, since people do not leave their homes then, so there is concealment in the matters that occur.

But in terminology, it is a term for knots, incantations, and medicines issued by the sorcerer through the agency of the devils, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Sulayman. Sulayman did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic and that which was revealed to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut﴾, meaning: and they taught them what was revealed to the two angels at Babylon. ﴿Harut and Marut﴾ are two names of angels. ﴿Yet they did not teach anyone until they said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve"﴾ [Al-Baqarah 102].

Therefore magic is often connected with the jinn, to the extent that the jinni speaks and says, "I cannot come out because I am bewitched," but if Allah, mighty and majestic, wills, the magic is discovered and destroyed, and then the patient is healed.

His saying ﴿obvious﴾ means clear and manifest, because (bana) and (abana) come with one meaning. You say: "The morning became clear" (bana al-subh) and "the morning became clear" (abana al-subh). (Abana) is quadriliteral, and (bana) is triliteral. (Bana) is said as bayyin, and (abana) is said as mubin, though (abana) may also be transitive, not with the meaning of (bana), as when you say: abana al-haqq, abana al-amr li, meaning: he made it manifest.

Let us return to this verse.

* In this verse: a demonstration of the obstinacy of those who denied the Messenger (ﷺ). The reason for this is that Allah mentions that if a scripture on paper were sent down to them and they touched it with their hands, they would say: this is magic, which is not correct.

The basis of this inference, though it may not be proper for me to call it an inference, is why Allah mentions this about them: because there came to them signs of the kind that human beings would believe in on their account, yet ﴿if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "This is continuous magic"﴾ [Al-Qamar 2]. So Allah knew from their condition that if matters reached the point of a scripture on paper, as they were accustomed to, which they touched with their hands, they would say: this is obvious magic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that if the scripture is on paper, it is clearer and more manifest; otherwise it could be written on other than paper, on what?
